evidence: Plaut. Truc. 5.13, as cited by Lewis & Short
terms.comment: Latin has no separate word for a cot: cūnae, the baby’s bed, from the root of ‘to lie’ (de Vaan 153), serves for both. For an older child’s own bed, lectulus.

Levi–Bini’s lecticulus (p. 37, s.v. lettino) is not in Lewis & Short, which has only lectīcula, a small litter. With bars, lectulus clāthrātus (clāthrō, to set with bars: Cato Agr. 4; Plaut. Mil. 2.4.26, Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: et sī quis deus mihi largiātur, ut ex hāc aetāte repuerāscam et in cūnīs vāgiam, valdē recūsem
phrases.english: and if some god were to grant that I should turn child again at my age and cry in the cradle, I should firmly refuse

sources: Lewis & Short: cunae · Lewis & Short: lectulus · Lewis & Short: lecticula · Lewis & Short: clathro

Michiel de Vaan, Etymological Dictionary of Latin and the other Italic Languages (2008), p. 153, s.v. cūnae. Enrico Levi and Arturo Bini, Il latino come lingua viva (1937), p. 37, s.v. lettino. Traupman and Morgan–Owens have no word for a cot (Morgan–Owens’s cot is the camp bed).
Cicero (Sen.) from the Latinitas loci collections.
